experiments.title: FCFS Scheduling
theory_points: FCFS is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm
Processes are executed in order of arrival using a FIFO queue
Non-preemptive — once a process starts, it runs until completion
Can cause convoy effect where short processes wait behind long ones
Turnaround time = Completion time - Arrival time
Waiting time = Turnaround time - Burst time

experiments.title: SJF Scheduling
theory_points: SJF selects the process with the smallest burst time next
Can be preemptive (SRTF) or non-preemptive
Provides minimum average waiting time among non-preemptive algorithms
Requires knowledge of burst time in advance (prediction based)
May cause starvation of long processes

experiments.title: Priority Scheduling
theory_points: Each process is assigned a priority value
CPU is allocated to the process with highest priority
Can be preemptive or non-preemptive
Lower number may mean higher priority (system dependent)
Starvation possible — solved using aging technique

experiments.title: Round Robin Scheduling
theory_points: Preemptive version of FCFS with a fixed time quantum
Each process gets CPU for one time quantum, then moves to back of queue
Performance depends heavily on time quantum size
Large quantum behaves like FCFS; very small quantum causes high context switching
Fair allocation — every process gets equal CPU time

experiments.title: Producer Consumer Problem
theory_points: Classic synchronization problem involving shared buffer
Producer generates data and places it in buffer
Consumer removes data from buffer for processing
Requires synchronization using semaphores or mutex
Uses three semaphores: mutex, full, empty
Demonstrates need for mutual exclusion and cooperation

experiments.title: Dining Philosophers Problem
theory_points: Five philosophers sit around a table with five chopsticks
Each philosopher needs two chopsticks to eat
Illustrates deadlock and resource allocation issues
Solutions include resource ordering, semaphores, or monitors
Demonstrates mutual exclusion and deadlock prevention

experiments.title: Reader Writer Problem
theory_points: Synchronization problem for shared database access
Multiple readers can read simultaneously
Writers need exclusive access — no other reader or writer allowed
Uses semaphores: mutex, wrt, and readcount variable
Variants: reader-priority, writer-priority, fair solution

experiments.title: Bankers Algorithm
theory_points: Deadlock avoidance algorithm proposed by Dijkstra
Checks if resource allocation leaves system in safe state
Uses Available, Max, Allocation, and Need matrices
Safe state means a safe sequence exists for all processes
Denies requests that would lead to unsafe state

experiments.title: FIFO Page Replacement
keywords: first in first out page replacement
theory_points: Simplest page replacement algorithm
Replaces the oldest page in memory (first loaded = first replaced)
Uses a FIFO queue to track page order
Suffers from Belady's anomaly — more frames can cause more faults
Easy to implement but not optimal

experiments.title: LRU Page Replacement
theory_points: Replaces the page that has not been used for the longest time
Based on locality of reference principle
Better performance than FIFO in most cases
Does not suffer from Belady's anomaly
Implementation methods: counters, stack, or reference bits

experiments.title: Optimal Page Replacement
theory_points: Replaces the page that will not be used for the longest time in future
Produces minimum number of page faults — theoretical best
Not implementable in practice (requires future knowledge)
Used as benchmark to compare other algorithms
Also known as Belady's Optimal algorithm

experiments.title: First Fit Memory Allocation
theory_points: Allocates the first memory block that is large enough
Searches from the beginning of memory each time
Fast allocation — stops at first suitable block
Can cause external fragmentation over time
Simple to implement using linked list of free blocks

experiments.title: Best Fit Memory Allocation
theory_points: Allocates the smallest block that is sufficient
Searches entire list to find closest size match
Minimizes wasted space in allocated block
Slower than first fit due to full list scan
Can create many small unusable fragments

experiments.title: Worst Fit Memory Allocation
theory_points: Allocates the largest available memory block
Idea: leftover fragment will be large enough for future use
Searches entire free list for maximum size block
Tends to break large blocks, reducing future flexibility
Generally poorest performance among the three strategies

experiments.title: FCFS Disk Scheduling
theory_points: Services disk I/O requests in order they arrive
Simple and fair but not optimal
Can result in large total head movement
No starvation — every request is served
Used as baseline to compare other disk algorithms

experiments.title: SSTF Disk Scheduling
theory_points: Selects the request closest to current head position
Reduces total seek time compared to FCFS
May cause starvation of distant requests
Similar concept to SJF in CPU scheduling
Not optimal but significantly better than FCFS

experiments.title: SCAN Disk Scheduling
theory_points: Head moves in one direction servicing all requests, then reverses
Also known as Elevator Algorithm
Provides more uniform wait times than SSTF
No starvation — all requests eventually served
Variant: C-SCAN (Circular SCAN) for more uniform response

experiments.title: Fork System Call
theory_points: fork() creates a new child process as copy of parent
Returns 0 to child, child PID to parent, -1 on failure
Child gets copy of parent's address space
Both processes execute concurrently after fork
Used with exec() to run different programs in child

experiments.title: Inter Process Communication
theory_points: IPC allows processes to communicate and synchronize
Methods: pipes, shared memory, message queues, signals
Pipes provide unidirectional data flow between processes
Shared memory is fastest IPC — processes access same memory region
Message queues allow structured message exchange
